summary.text: 爱 is the simplified form of 愛, the character used for love and affection. The modern shape includes 友 at the bottom, but this graphic change does not show that the older character meant “friend.”

formation.text: 愛’s graphic history includes an early form written 㤅, with 心 as a meaning-bearing element and an upper element identified variously as 兂 or 旡 and proposed as phonetic. Qin-type forms add 夊, associated with walking. These forms do not establish a single complete sequence leading to 爱.

components.text: In early 㤅, 心 contributes the heart or feeling category. It belongs to the history of 愛, not to the visible components of modern 爱.
The upper element in early 㤅 is identified as 兂 in one analysis and 旡 in another, and is proposed as phonetic. Its identity and sound role remain unsettled; neither form is the visible top of 爱.

sound_limitation.text: The cited accounts give reconstructions for 愛 but no sound comparison for 兂 or 旡 as the proposed phonetic element in 㤅.

components.text: Qin-type forms of 愛 add 夊, interpreted as a walking element; the received Shuowen analysis also includes it. It is not identified as a replacement for another component.

友 is visible at the bottom of 爱. The simplified form is described as a cursive-derived regularization, and one account says 友 replaces the former lower portion. This does not establish an ancient meaning or sound role for 友 in 愛; the precise graphic pathway remains unresolved.

history.text: The selected bronze-style image is a modern rendering of an early 㤅-type form; the seal-style image renders 愛 in the received Shuowen tradition, associated with a Qin-type form. They show distinct forms without proving a complete lineage.

Historical accounts describe early bronze forms with 心 and an upper element, while Qin-type forms add 夊. Regional forms varied and could coexist; the earliest physical attestation and a universal sequence are unresolved.
爱 is described as a cursive-derived regularization of 愛 and was officially adopted in 1956. That adoption date does not establish when the shape first arose.

uncertainties.text: The upper element in 㤅 is identified as either 兂 or 旡, and its proposed phonetic role lacks a sound comparison for either form.
Early 㤅 is glossed as benevolence, while the Shuowen tradition glosses 愛 as an appearance of walking; later examples use 愛 for affection. How and when 愛 took on that use is unresolved.

Proposed connections between the spoken word 愛 and other Sino-Tibetan words, and a separate proposal linking it with breath or inhalation vocabulary, remain disputed hypotheses about the word rather than explanations of the graph.

senses.text: A Warring States Zhongshan bronze use is cited with the graph 㤅 in an affection-related expression. Transmitted literary examples also use 愛 for affection, but they do not establish the earliest physical witness or a precise date for this sense.
愛 is used for love, affection, fondness, and liking. The evidence does not establish a dated sequence among these current glosses.

limitations.text: Early 㤅 is associated with benevolence, while later examples use 愛 for affection. The transition is not securely dated, and the evidence does not settle whether it involved borrowing, replacement, or another process; no development is asserted.

overview.text: 爱 is the simplified form of 愛, used for love and affection. Its visible 友 reflects a later graphic change, not an ancient meaning of “friend.”

components.text: In early 㤅, 心 contributes the heart or feeling category; it belongs to 愛’s history, not as a separate part of modern 爱.
The upper element in early 㤅 is disputed between 兂 and 旡. It is proposed as a sound element, but its sound relationship remains unsettled.
Qin-type and received seal-script forms of 愛 include 夊, associated with walking.
友 appears in the simplified shape after graphic regularization; it does not establish an ancient meaning or sound role.

relationships.text: In the early 㤅 analysis, 心 contributes the heart or feeling category.
One analysis identifies 兂 as the proposed phonetic element in early 㤅; another identifies 旡. No sound comparison establishes this relationship here.
An alternative analysis identifies 旡 as the proposed phonetic element in early 㤅. The competing identification and lack of a sound comparison leave this analysis unsettled.
Qin-type forms add 夊, interpreted as a walking element; the Shuowen analysis also includes it in 愛.
One account describes the simplified form as replacing the lower portion with 友. Its shape is also described as cursive-derived regularization, but the full pathway is not documented.
爱 is the officially adopted simplified form of 愛; its shape is described as cursive-derived regularization.
Early bronze forms of 愛 are described as 㤅, while Qin-type forms add 夊. This connects the historical 㤅 form to the graphic history of 愛 without asserting a single universal lineage.
